verses.text: On the third day a wedding took place at Cana in Galilee. Jesus' mother was there,
and Jesus and His disciples had also been invited to the wedding.
When the wine ran out, Jesus' mother said to Him, "They have no more wine."
"Woman, what is that to you and to Me?" Jesus replied. "My hour has not yet come."
His mother said to the servants, "Do whatever He tells you."
Now six stone water jars had been set there for the Jewish rites of purification. Each could hold from twenty to thirty gallons.
Jesus told the servants, "Fill the jars with water." So they filled them to the brim.
"Now draw some out," He said, "and take it to the master of the banquet." They did so,
and the master of the banquet tasted the water that had been turned into wine. He did not know where it was from, but the servants who had drawn the water knew. Then he called the bridegroom aside
and said, "Everyone serves the fine wine first, and then the cheap wine after the guests are drunk. But you have saved the fine wine until now!"
Jesus performed this, the first of His signs, at Cana in Galilee. He thus revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him.
After this, He went down to Capernaum with His mother and brothers and His disciples, and they stayed there a few days.
When the Jewish Passover was near, Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
In the temple courts He found men selling cattle, sheep, and doves, and money changers seated at their tables.
So He made a whip out of cords and drove all from the temple courts, both sheep and cattle. He poured out the coins of the money changers and overturned their tables.
To those selling doves He said, "Get these out of here! How dare you turn My Father's house into a marketplace!"
His disciples remembered that it is written: "Zeal for Your house will consume Me."
On account of this, the Jews demanded, "What sign can You show us to prove Your authority to do these things?"
Jesus answered, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again."
"This temple took forty-six years to build," the Jews replied, "and You are going to raise it up in three days?"
But Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body.
After He was raised from the dead, His disciples remembered that He had said this. Then they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
While He was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many people saw the signs He was doing and believed in His name.
But Jesus did not entrust Himself to them, for He knew them all.
He did not need any testimony about man, for He knew what was in a man.

context.author: Traditionally the apostle John
context.genre: Theological narrative — the first of John's seven chosen signs, paired with a second, very different act of authority
context.audience: A broad, likely mixed Jewish and Gentile readership toward the end of the first century
context.setting: Cana was a small, unremarkable Galilean village — even Nathanael's own hometown per John 21:2 — a fitting, humble setting for the very first public sign Jesus performs. The chapter then shifts abruptly to Jerusalem's temple courts at Passover, when the city's population swelled dramatically with pilgrims.
context.custom: The six stone water jars were specifically for Jewish ceremonial washing — stone was preferred because, unlike clay, it couldn't contract ritual impurity. Money changers exchanged ordinary coinage for the Tyrian silver required for the temple tax, and animal sellers supplied pilgrims with sacrifices vetted on-site — legitimate services that had crowded out the Court of the Gentiles' actual purpose.
context.timelineImmediate: John pairs two very different demonstrations of authority back to back — a quiet, celebratory miracle at a village wedding, followed immediately by a public, forceful confrontation in the temple itself, both in the opening days of Jesus' ministry as John tells it.
context.timelineBible: Jesus' answer, "destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up," is directly clarified by John himself as referring to His own body — a claim whose full meaning wouldn't be understood until after the resurrection actually happened.
context.sparkNotes: Jesus turns water into wine at a wedding in Cana, the first of the seven signs John builds his whole Gospel around, then travels to Jerusalem where He drives the money changers from the temple with a whip of cords. When challenged for a sign to justify this, Jesus answers cryptically that He will raise a destroyed temple in three days — a claim John explains was really about His own body and resurrection, understood only in hindsight.

translation.meaning: Not just a miracle for its own sake, but a pointer toward a deeper truth about who Jesus is — John structures his entire Gospel around seven such signs.

occurrences.note: John himself states his purpose directly near the book's end: these signs are written — so that readers — may believe (20:30-31).

translation.meaning: Passionate devotion or jealousy for something's honor — quoted directly from Psalm 69:9 by the disciples as they watch Jesus overturn the temple's tables.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's account of a temple cleansing, placed in the final week rather than the start of Jesus' ministry — whether this is the same event told out of sequence, or two separate cleansings, is genuinely debated among readers.
Mark's version of the same later temple cleansing.

otBackground.note: "Zeal for Your house will consume me" — quoted directly by the disciples as they recall this scene.
"A house of prayer for all nations" — the standard Jesus' action restores against the temple's commercialized Court of the Gentiles.
The Lord suddenly coming to His temple to purify it — background for Jesus' unannounced, forceful arrival.

commentary.note: Henry notes Mary's approach carefully: she doesn't tell Jesus what to do, only states the need — 'they have no wine' — leaving the how entirely to Him. He reads her instruction to the servants, 'whatsoever he saith unto you, do it,' as good counsel for anyone who wants Christ present at their own affairs: don't prescribe the method, just obey whatever He actually says.

Gill works out the real scale of the miracle: six jars holding twenty to thirty gallons each comes to somewhere around one hundred twenty to one hundred eighty gallons of wine — enough, by some contemporary estimates, for over a hundred guests. He notes weddings in this period commonly lasted a full week, making such a large, sudden supply a genuinely practical provision, not excess for its own sake.

Clarke reads Jesus' address to Mary, 'Woman,' as carrying no coldness in the original — a perfectly respectful and even affectionate title in that culture, the same word He later uses to Mary from the cross itself (19:26). He treats her confidence in instructing the servants as a sign of quiet, settled faith, not presumption.

overview.summary: At a wedding in Cana Jesus turns water into wine, His first sign. He goes to Jerusalem for Passover, drives the sellers from the temple, and says the temple of His body will be raised in three days.
overview.settingLine: Cana in Galilee, then the Jerusalem temple.

history.t: Weddings lasted days, and running out of wine shamed the host.
Herod's temple had been under construction for forty-six years.

customs.t: Large stone jars held water for ritual washing, since stone stayed pure.
The master of the feast served the best wine first, which Jesus' wine reversed.

archaeology.t: Khirbet Qana, a ruin north of Nazareth, is a leading candidate for ancient Cana.
Carved stone jars are common finds in Jewish homes of this era.

overview.discussion: John calls the water into wine a sign. What do you think it points to about who Jesus is?
overview.book: The fourth Gospel · 21 chapters. Written so readers would believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.
overview.author: John
